sections.title: The town on a burning floor
sections.intro_md:
In 1916 a fire was noticed in the Bhowrah colliery near Jharia, in what is now Dhanbad district. Nobody put it out. More than a hundred years later the coal under Jharia is still burning. By 1972 more than 70 separate fires had been mapped. Smoke leaks through cracks in the roads, houses tilt as the ground sinks, and in June 2025 the Union Cabinet approved a fresh 5,940 crore rupee plan to move the families who live on top of it.

That is Jharkhand in one picture. The state sits on some of the richest ground in India: it produces more than 40 percent of the country's minerals, its only prime coking coal and its first uranium. It is also one of the poorest states, and a quarter of its people are Adivasi, the original peoples of these forests, who fought the British longer and harder than almost anyone.

Today you meet the waterfalls, the rebels, the steel city, the painted houses and the dance with masks.

sections.title: Where you are
sections.intro_md:
Jharkhand means 'land of forests'. It lies in eastern India, with Bihar to the north, West Bengal to the east, Odisha to the south, and Chhattisgarh and Uttar Pradesh to the west. It covers 79,716 square kilometres, slightly smaller than Austria, and almost all of it is the Chota Nagpur Plateau.

The state was carved out of southern Bihar on 15 November 2000, the birth anniversary of Birsa Munda, and became India's 28th state. The capital is Ranchi. The biggest city is Jamshedpur, the steel town. Dhanbad is the coal capital, Bokaro the second steel city, Deoghar the pilgrim town.

The 2011 Census counted 32,988,134 people in 24 districts. About 76 percent live in villages. Scheduled Tribes were 26.2 percent, around 8.6 million people from 32 recognised communities. The official language is Hindi, with 16 more given second-language status, from Santali and Mundari to Bengali and Urdu.

sections.title: The plateau and its waterfalls
sections.intro_md:
The Chota Nagpur Plateau is old rock, some of it more than three billion years old, worn into a staircase of flat tablelands. Ranchi sits on the top step at about 600 metres. Wherever a river falls off a step, there is a waterfall, which is why Ranchi district alone has Hundru, Dassam, Jonha and a dozen smaller falls within an hour's drive.

The rivers run in every direction: the Damodar and Barakar east to Bengal, the Subarnarekha south-east to the Bay of Bengal, the North Koel north to the Son and the Ganga, the South Koel and Sankh south into Odisha. Under the plateau lie coal seams in the Damodar valley, iron ore in Singhbhum, copper at Ghatshila, mica at Koderma and uranium at Jaduguda.

Forest covers about 30 percent of the state: sal, mahua, palash and bamboo. Sal is the state tree and palash, the 'flame of the forest' that turns hillsides orange in March, is the state flower. The Asian elephant is the state animal.

spotlights.name: Hundru Falls
spotlights.spot_it: A wide river dropping off a ledge of dark rock into a pool ringed by boulders, about 45 km from Ranchi.
spotlights.story_md: The Subarnarekha, the 'river with streaks of gold', drops about 98 metres here, off the edge of the Ranchi plateau. In the monsoon the falls are a single roaring sheet. In winter they split into separate strands, and the rocks below, carved into potholes and smooth channels by centuries of water, become a picnic ground. The river's name is not just poetry: villagers downstream have panned its sand for flecks of gold for generations, a small trade still recorded in the 2000s. Hundru is the waterfall most visitors to Ranchi see first.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The signature landscape of the Ranchi plateau, and the reason it is called a city of waterfalls.
spotlights.memory_hook: A golden river jumping off a 98-metre step.

spotlights.name: Dassam Falls

where.label: Kanchi river near Taimara, Ranchi district

spotlights.spot_it: A horseshoe of falls on a forested river, water pouring in several streams over a curved rock wall about 44 metres high.
spotlights.story_md: Locals also call it Dassam Ghagh, ghagh being the word for a waterfall. The Kanchi river, a tributary of the Subarnarekha, falls about 44 metres in a curving cliff, so you see the water from the side as well as the front. The pool below looks calm and is not: Dassam has a long record of drownings, and the district administration posts warnings and lifeguards in season. The surrounding land is Munda country, and the falls sit on routes that pilgrims and traders have used for centuries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the most photographed falls in eastern India, and one of the most dangerous to swim.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten streams pour, and the calm pool lies.

spotlights.name: Lodh Falls
spotlights.spot_it: A very tall, narrow fall in tiers through deep forest, heard long before it is seen.
spotlights.story_md: Lodh, also called Budha Ghagh, is Jharkhand's highest waterfall, about 143 metres from top to bottom, where the Burha river tumbles off the Netarhat plateau inside the Palamau Tiger Reserve. The noise carries for kilometres in the monsoon. Getting there means a drive through Maoist-affected forest that kept tourists away for years; the security situation has improved sharply since 2023. Lodh is a reminder that the plateau's best scenery is in its least visited corners.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The state's tallest fall, in the deepest forest.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hear Lodh first, see it later.

spotlights.name: Netarhat
spotlights.when: Hill station since the British era
spotlights.spot_it: A cool flat-topped plateau over 1,100 metres high, pine trees, and crowds at a cliff edge at sunset.
spotlights.story_md: Netarhat, called the 'Queen of Chota Nagpur', is a plateau about 1,128 metres up where British officials built bungalows to escape the summer heat. It is famous for two things. One is Magnolia Point, a sunset viewpoint tied to a local legend about a British officer's daughter and a cowherd boy; the story has no documentary trace and is best treated as folklore. The other is the Netarhat Residential School, founded in 1954 as a free public boarding school for gifted children, which for decades topped the Bihar board exams and produced a long list of civil servants.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Jharkhand's best-known hill station and the home of a legendary school.
spotlights.memory_hook: A plateau that grows pine trees and IAS officers.

spotlights.name: Betla and the Palamau Tiger Reserve
spotlights.spot_it: Sal forest, grassy clearings with gaur and spotted deer, and the ruined Chero forts on a nearby hill.
spotlights.story_md: Palamau was one of India's first nine tiger reserves when Project Tiger began in 1973. It also has a strange claim: in 1932 a forest officer, J. W. Nicholson, carried out what is often called the world's first tiger census here, counting pugmarks. Betla National Park is its heart, with elephants, gaur, sloth bears and peafowl. The tigers themselves have nearly gone. Recent national estimates found only one or a handful in Palamau, blamed on poaching, cattle grazing and years of insurgency in the forest. Sightings since 2023 have raised hopes of recolonisation.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A founding tiger reserve that has almost lost its tigers.
spotlights.memory_hook: First to count tigers, nearly the first to lose them.

spotlights.name: Dalma hills and the elephants
spotlights.spot_it: Forested hills rising behind the Jamshedpur skyline, with elephant herds that cross into Bengal and Odisha.
spotlights.story_md: Dalma Wildlife Sanctuary, declared in 1975, covers about 193 square kilometres of hills just outside the steel city. It is best known for its elephants, the state animal, which move in seasonal routes between Jharkhand, West Bengal and Odisha. Those routes now cross highways, railways and mines, and Jharkhand records some of India's worst human-elephant conflict: in many years more than 80 people are killed by elephants in the state, and elephants die on rail lines and from electrocution. Dalma is where you see how close industry and wilderness sit here.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The elephant forest at the edge of the biggest industrial city.
spotlights.memory_hook: Steel city on one side, elephant road on the other.

spotlights.name: Saranda, the forest of seven hundred hills
spotlights.spot_it: Endless rolling hills of sal forest, red mine roads cut into them, iron ore dust on the leaves.
spotlights.story_md: Saranda means 'seven hundred hills' in Ho. Its roughly 820 square kilometres hold one of Asia's largest sal forests, and underneath, some of India's richest iron ore, mined by SAIL at Kiriburu and Meghahatuburu since the 1960s. For years it was also a Maoist stronghold. On 13 November 2025 the Supreme Court ordered Jharkhand to notify a large part of Saranda as a wildlife sanctuary and banned mining inside it and within one kilometre of its boundary, while protecting the forest rights of Ho villagers. Forest, ore, rebels and tribal rights all meet here.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The test case for whether India can keep a great forest on top of great ore.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven hundred hills, one iron question.

spotlights.name: The Damodar and its dams
spotlights.spot_it: A broad river held back by long earth-and-concrete dams, coal country all around.
spotlights.story_md: The Damodar used to flood lower Bengal so often that it was called the 'Sorrow of Bengal'. In 1948 India created the Damodar Valley Corporation, modelled on America's Tennessee Valley Authority, as the new country's first multipurpose river valley project: dams for flood control, irrigation and power. Maithon, completed in 1957, has an underground power station, one of the first in India. The Damodar also runs through the coal belt of Jharia, Bokaro and Ramgarh, and today it carries some of the heaviest industrial pollution of any river in the region.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Independent India's first big river valley project began here.
spotlights.memory_hook: The sorrow of Bengal, tamed into a power grid.

sections.title: The peoples of Jharkhand
sections.intro_md:
Adivasi means 'first inhabitants'. In Jharkhand there are 32 Scheduled Tribes, and four of them make up most of the tribal population: Santhals, Oraons, Mundas and Hos. They speak languages from two families that are not related to Hindi at all. Santali, Mundari and Ho are Austroasiatic, distant cousins of Khmer and Vietnamese. Kurukh, the language of the Oraons, is Dravidian, related to Tamil and Kannada.

The 2011 Census found that Jharkhand's tribal share had been falling for a century, from over a third of the region's people in 1951 to 26.2 percent, as miners, steel workers and traders moved in and Adivasis moved out to find work. That shift is the root of Jharkhand politics: land laws, statehood, the Sarna religion code and the fight over who gets jobs.

Non-tribal Jharkhand is just as mixed: Kurmi Mahtos, Bhumij, Bengalis in the east, Maithili and Magahi speakers in the north, and Bihari migrants in every city.

spotlights.name: Santhals
spotlights.spot_it: Mud houses painted in bands of colour, women in white saris with red or green checks, line dances to the tamak drum.
spotlights.story_md: The Santhals are Jharkhand's largest tribe, about 2.75 million in the state in 2011, and one of the largest in India. They live mostly in the north-east, the Santhal Parganas, a district carved out after their 1855 revolt. Santhal villages are known for neat lanes, decorated walls and a headman, the manjhi, who sits with the elders at the village's sacred site. Their language, Santali, got its own script, Ol Chiki, in 1925, and the President of India, Droupadi Murmu, is a Santhal from Odisha.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The biggest Adivasi community, with the strongest written-language movement.
spotlights.memory_hook: One revolt, one script, one President.

spotlights.name: Mundas
spotlights.when: Settled the plateau over 2,000 years ago (estimated)
spotlights.spot_it: Stone slabs standing upright at village edges, marking graves and land, and the word 'Johar' as a greeting.
spotlights.story_md: The Mundas think of themselves as the people who cleared the forest of Chota Nagpur. The founding families of a village, the khuntkattidars, held the land collectively, and their ancestors are buried under stone slabs called sasandiri, while upright memorial stones mark lineage and land. That idea, land as inheritance from the dead, sits behind Birsa Munda's revolt and the 1908 Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act. Their greeting 'Johar' is now used across Jharkhand by people of every background.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The people whose idea of land shaped Jharkhand's laws.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ancestors under stone, land that cannot be sold.

spotlights.name: Oraons (Kurukh)
spotlights.when: Dravidian speakers of the north plateau
spotlights.spot_it: Big village festivals with the karam branch in the dance ground, and the Kurukh language, a southern tongue in the north.
spotlights.story_md: The Oraons call themselves Kurukh and speak a Dravidian language, which puzzles first-time visitors: their nearest linguistic relatives are in Karnataka. Oral tradition says their ancestors came from the Rohtas plateau and before that from the south. They are known for the dhumkuria, the village youth dormitory, for village confederations called parhas, and for the Karam and Sarhul festivals. Many Oraons converted to Christianity in the 19th century, and the community has produced a long line of hockey players from Gumla and Simdega.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A Dravidian island in the middle of north India.
spotlights.memory_hook: They live in Jharkhand and talk like Karnataka.

spotlights.name: Hos
spotlights.spot_it: Villages in the iron hills of Singhbhum, a script of their own, and the Mage Parab festival in January.
spotlights.story_md: The Hos live in the Kolhan, the iron and forest country around Chaibasa. They fought the British in the Kol uprising of 1831 and 1832. Afterwards Captain Thomas Wilkinson left their own government in place: village heads (mundas) and regional heads (mankis) kept collecting revenue and settling disputes under 'Wilkinson's Rule' of 1837, a system still partly alive. In the 1950s Lako Bodra created the Warang Citi script for the Ho language. Their great festival is Mage Parab, after the harvest.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A people the British had to govern through their own chiefs.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mundas and mankis, ruling the iron hills.

spotlights.name: Asurs, the iron smelters
spotlights.spot_it: Small hamlets on the high plateau; older men who still remember smelting iron in clay furnaces.
spotlights.story_md: The Asurs are one of Jharkhand's smallest tribes, around 22,000 people in 2011, classed as a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group. Their traditional craft was smelting iron from ore in small clay furnaces worked by bellows, a technology that made them sought after across the plateau. Industrial steel ended it in the 20th century. They share a name with the demons of Hindu epics and some Asur activists reject the celebration of Durga killing Mahishasura, whom they regard as an ancestor. In the late 2010s young Asurs started Asur Adivasi Mobile Radio, a phone-based station, to keep their language alive.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Living carriers of an old metal technology and a counter-story to a famous myth.
spotlights.memory_hook: The 'demons' of the epics were the smiths of the hills.

sections.title: Rock art, megaliths and forest kings
sections.intro_md:
Jharkhand's past is written on stone more than in archives. Painted rock shelters around Hazaribagh go back thousands of years. Megaliths, upright stones raised for the dead, are still being set up by Munda and Ho families today, which makes the region one of the few places on earth where a megalithic tradition never stopped.

In the old Sanskrit texts this was Jharikhanda or Kikata, a wild frontier. The Mughals called it Kokrah and valued it for diamonds from its rivers. Real power on the plateau lay with local dynasties: the Nagvanshis of Chota Nagpur, who claimed to have ruled from the first century CE until zamindari was abolished in the 1950s, the Cheros of Palamu, and the Rajas of Ramgarh and Singhbhum. They paid tribute to Delhi when forced to and ignored it when they could.

The British arrived after 1765, when the East India Company got the revenue rights of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, and that is when the trouble began.

spotlights.name: Isko rock art
spotlights.spot_it: Red ochre figures, animals and geometric mazes on an overhanging rock face above a stream.
spotlights.story_md: Isko is a rock shelter near Barkagaon in Hazaribagh, with hundreds of motifs painted in red and white: animals, plants, human figures and dense geometric patterns. The writer and conservationist Bulu Imam reported it to state archaeologists in 1991. Its age is disputed: estimates range from the Mesolithic, around 10,000 years ago, to the Chalcolithic. What makes Isko special is that the women of the surrounding villages still paint very similar patterns on their mud houses for Sohrai and Khovar. Few places show such a direct line between prehistoric art and living art.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Possibly the oldest picture gallery in Jharkhand, with descendants still painting.
spotlights.memory_hook: Painted on rock 10,000 years ago, painted on mud walls last Diwali.

spotlights.name: Maluti temples
spotlights.when: Built over roughly the 17th to 19th centuries
spotlights.spot_it: Dozens of small brick temples with curved roofs packed into one village, their walls covered in terracotta panels.
spotlights.story_md: Maluti was the seat of the Baj Basanta rajas, small kings who were granted the land tax-free by the sultan of Bengal. They and their branches kept building temples, each family adding its own. There were once 108. Today 72 survive, many of them in the Bengal style with curved roofs and baked-brick panels showing the Ramayana, the Mahabharata, Durga killing the buffalo demon and scenes of daily life. In 2010 the Global Heritage Fund listed Maluti among 12 sites in the developing world 'on the verge' of irreparable loss. Conservation has been slow.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The densest cluster of terracotta temples in eastern India outside Bengal.
spotlights.memory_hook: A village with 108 temples, now 72 and counting down.

spotlights.name: Palamu forts
spotlights.spot_it: Two ruined stone forts on wooded hills above the Auranga river, with arched gates swallowed by jungle.
spotlights.story_md: The Cheros ruled Palamu from the 16th century. Their greatest king, Medini Rai, extended the kingdom in the mid-17th century, and the old fort on the plain and the new fort on the hill are linked to the Chero rajas of his era. The Mughals attacked Palamu several times; Aurangzeb's governor Daud Khan finally took it in 1660. The forts now sit inside the tiger reserve near Betla, and the jungle has been pulling them apart for three centuries. The 'Nagpuri gate' of the new fort is the best preserved part.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The remains of a forest kingdom that held off the Mughals for decades.
spotlights.memory_hook: Forts the jungle is slowly winning back.

spotlights.name: Navratangarh, the diamond king's palace
spotlights.spot_it: A five-storey stone palace in a remote village, with temples and step-wells around it.
spotlights.story_md: The Nagvanshi king Durjan Shah refused to pay tribute to Jahangir and spent about 12 years as a prisoner in Gwalior fort. The story goes that he won his freedom by proving himself an expert on diamonds: he could tell a real stone from a fake when the court jewellers could not. The rivers of his kingdom were known for diamonds, which is why the Mughals cared about it at all. Back home he built Navratangarh at Doisa, a five-storey palace whose name means 'nine jewels', with temples and a fort around it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The best surviving palace of the dynasty that ruled the plateau for centuries.
spotlights.memory_hook: A king who bought his freedom with his eye for diamonds.

sections.title: A century of revolts
sections.intro_md:
British rule reached the plateau through the land. The Permanent Settlement of 1793 turned local chiefs into landlords who owed fixed cash revenue. Outsiders, called dikus, arrived as moneylenders, contractors and new landlords. Adivasi land, held by lineages for generations without paper titles, began to pass to strangers through debt, forced labour and the courts.

The result was more than a century of risings. The Paharias of the Rajmahal hills fought in the 1770s and 1780s. The Kol uprising of 1831 and 1832 united Mundas, Hos and Oraons. The Santhal Hul of 1855 was one of the biggest rebellions in British India before 1857. Birsa Munda's Ulgulan of 1899 and 1900 was the last great one. Each was crushed, and each forced a new law: special districts, protected tenancies, and in 1908 the Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act, which still bans most sales of tribal land to non-tribals.

Historians argue about how 'first' these were. Jharkhand does not: here they are the independence movement.

spotlights.name: Tilka Manjhi
spotlights.spot_it: A statue of a young man drawing a bow, in Dumka, Bhagalpur and Jamshedpur.
spotlights.story_md: Tilka Manjhi, a Paharia leader of the Rajmahal hills, is remembered as the first Adivasi to take up arms against the Company. In 1784, the story goes, he shot Augustus Cleveland, the British collector of Bhagalpur, with an arrow; Cleveland died soon after. Tilka was captured and, by tradition, tied to the tail of a horse, dragged to Bhagalpur and hanged from a banyan tree in 1785. Colonial records tell a thinner story and some historians doubt he killed Cleveland, who died at sea on his way home. Bhagalpur's university is named after him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first name in Jharkhand's roll of rebels.
spotlights.memory_hook: An arrow in 1784, a university name today.

spotlights.name: The Santhal Hul
spotlights.spot_it: Victorian engravings of Santhal archers fighting sepoys, and statues of two brothers on every Santhal Parganas crossroad.
spotlights.story_md: On 30 June 1855 thousands of Santhals gathered at Bhognadih and declared Hul, rebellion, under four brothers: Sidhu, Kanhu, Chand and Bhairav Murmu, with their sisters Phulo and Jhano. They marched against moneylenders, landlords and Company police, and for a time ran their own administration. The British declared martial law in November and used troops, elephants and burning of villages. Estimates of the dead run from 10,000 to over 15,000. The Illustrated London News printed engravings of the fighting for readers in Britain. 30 June is now Hul Diwas, a state holiday.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The rebellion that created the Santhal Parganas and its protective laws.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four brothers, two sisters, one word: Hul.

spotlights.name: Birsa Munda, Dharti Aba
spotlights.spot_it: A young man with long hair, a turban and a cloth wrap: the only surviving photograph, taken after his arrest.
spotlights.story_md: Birsa Munda was born in Ulihatu in 1875, studied at a German mission school and took the name Birsa David. He left the church, began preaching a reformed Munda faith of one god, no alcohol and no sacrifice, and was called Dharti Aba, 'father of the earth'. At Christmas 1899 his followers attacked police stations and missions in the Ulgulan, the great tumult. Troops broke them at Dombari Buru in January 1900. Birsa was captured on 3 February 1900 and died in Ranchi jail on 9 June 1900, aged about 25. His birthday is now the state's birthday and, since 2021, India's Janjatiya Gaurav Divas.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The man whose revolt gave Jharkhand its land law and its founding date.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dead at 25; his birthday is a state's birthday.

spotlights.name: The Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act, 1908
spotlights.spot_it: Every land deal in tribal Jharkhand still has to pass its test: can this land be transferred to a non-tribal?
spotlights.story_md: Passed eight years after Birsa's death, the CNT Act recognised khuntkatti, the collective land rights of founding Munda lineages, and restricted transfer of tribal land to non-tribals except with official permission. A sister law, the Santhal Parganas Tenancy Act, does the same in the north-east. These two laws are why Jharkhand land politics is different from anywhere else. In 2016 the state government tried to amend both to make it easier to use tribal land for roads and industry; mass protests followed and the Governor returned the bills in 2017.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Still the most fought-over law in Jharkhand.
spotlights.memory_hook: A law written because of a revolt, defended by protests a century later.

spotlights.name: Tana Bhagats
spotlights.spot_it: Men and women in white homespun, worshipping a tricolour flag with a spinning wheel on it at their courtyard shrine.
spotlights.story_md: In 1914 an Oraon man named Jatra Bhagat began preaching an end to spirit worship, sacrifice and liquor, and a refusal to pay rent or work as forced labour. His followers, the Tana Bhagats, later joined Gandhi's movement and adopted khadi and the charkha. Many lost their land to colonial auction for refusing to pay tax. They still wear white, still keep a Congress-era tricolour with a charkha at a shrine in their courtyards, and still ask the government to return the land their grandparents forfeited for the freedom struggle.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A living community that still worships the national movement.
spotlights.memory_hook: They pray to the charkha flag every morning.

sections.title: The 50-year road to a state
sections.intro_md:
The demand for a separate Jharkhand is older than independent India. In 1939 the Adivasi Mahasabha, led by Jaipal Singh Munda, asked for a tribal province carved from the Chota Nagpur and Santhal Parganas regions. The States Reorganisation Commission rejected it in 1955, saying no single language united the area.

The movement came back in the 1970s, now with the Jharkhand Mukti Morcha, coal-field trade unions, Kurmi Mahto farmers and students. Its methods ranged from elections to economic blockades. In 1995 Bihar created a Jharkhand Area Autonomous Council, which satisfied nobody. Finally, the Bihar Reorganisation Act passed Parliament in August 2000 and Jharkhand was born on 15 November 2000. The first Chief Minister was Babulal Marandi.

The new state had a rough start: 13 governments and three spells of President's rule in its first 20 years. In 2006 Madhu Koda, an independent MLA, became Chief Minister, a rare event in India, and later went to jail in a mining-licence corruption case.

spotlights.name: Jaipal Singh Munda, Marang Gomke
spotlights.spot_it: A tall man in the 1928 Indian Olympic team photo, the captain of the first Indian team to win hockey gold.
spotlights.story_md: Jaipal Singh Munda was a Munda boy sent by missionaries from Ranchi to St John's College, Oxford, where he won a hockey Blue. In 1928 he captained India at the Amsterdam Olympics; he left the squad after the group stage after a row with the English manager, so he was not on the field when India won gold. Later he taught in the Gold Coast, led the Adivasi Mahasabha and sat in the Constituent Assembly, where he told members that Adivasis had been treated badly for 6,000 years and asked for a new chapter. Jharkhandis call him Marang Gomke, 'great leader'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Olympic captain, Oxford man and the first voice for Jharkhand.
spotlights.memory_hook: From Oxford hockey to the Constituent Assembly floor.

spotlights.name: Shibu Soren, Dishom Guru
spotlights.spot_it: A white-bearded man in a white kurta and a green JMM scarf, addressed by supporters as 'Guruji'.
spotlights.story_md: Shibu Soren's father, a teacher, was murdered in 1957, reportedly by moneylenders' men. Shibu began by organising Santhals against moneylenders and land grabs, and co-founded the Jharkhand Mukti Morcha in the early 1970s. He was a Union Coal Minister, three times Chief Minister of Jharkhand for short spells, and a figure of both devotion and controversy, convicted in a murder case in 2006 and acquitted on appeal. He died in Delhi on 4 August 2025, aged 81. His son Hemant Soren is the current Chief Minister.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The face of the statehood movement for half a century.
spotlights.memory_hook: The land of forests' guru, gone at 81.

sections.title: Coal, steel and uranium
sections.intro_md:
Jharkhand is the clearest Indian case of what economists call the resource curse. The state produces more than 40 percent of India's minerals by most counts, and holds roughly a quarter of the country's coal and iron ore reserves. It has India's only prime coking coal at Jharia, the first uranium mine at Jaduguda, copper at Ghatshila, bauxite on the Netarhat plateau and, in Koderma and Giridih, what was once the world's biggest mica belt.

On top of that geology the Tatas built India's first big steel works in 1907 to 1912, the Soviet Union helped build Bokaro in the 1960s, and the Damodar valley became a chain of dams, power plants and coal washeries. Yet in 2011 about 39 percent of Jharkhandis lived below the poverty line, and NITI Aayog's 2023 multidimensional poverty index still put it among the three poorest states. Profits and royalties flowed to companies and the Centre; displacement, dust and land loss stayed local. That gap explains most of Jharkhand's politics.

spotlights.name: Jharia, the coalfield on fire
spotlights.spot_it: Open pits with flames and smoke in broad daylight, people carrying baskets of coal on their heads, cracked earth that steams.
spotlights.story_md: Jharia holds India's best coking coal, the kind needed to make steel. Underground fires, first noticed in 1916, spread through old workings as private owners left pillars of coal and open shafts. By 2007 an estimated 37 million tonnes of coal had burned and more than 400,000 people lived on land at risk of collapse. The 2009 master plan to move them largely stalled, with families resettled at Belgaria complaining of no work. In June 2025 the Centre approved a revised plan worth 5,940 crore rupees, with a livelihood grant for every family. Thousands still pick coal from the fires to sell.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's steel industry depends on coal from under a burning town.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hundred years on fire and still being mined.

spotlights.name: Tata Steel and Jamshedpur
spotlights.spot_it: A skyline of blast furnaces and chimneys beside the Subarnarekha, and a planned city of green avenues around it.
spotlights.story_md: Jamsetji Tata dreamed of an Indian steel plant but died in 1904. His son Dorabji and the geologist P. N. Bose found the site at Sakchi, where iron ore, coal, water and a railway met. Tata Iron and Steel Company was set up in 1907 and poured its first ingot in 1912. In 1919 the town was renamed Jamshedpur. The company ran the city's water, roads and power, and still does, which is why Jamshedpur has no elected municipal corporation. The firm introduced an eight-hour day in 1912 and maternity benefits in 1928, long before Indian law required them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's first planned industrial city and its oldest big steel works.
spotlights.memory_hook: A city named after a man who never saw it.

spotlights.name: Jaduguda uranium mine
spotlights.spot_it: Hills near Ghatshila with a mine headframe, a mill and long tailing ponds by tribal villages.
spotlights.story_md: Uranium was found at Jaduguda in 1951, and in 1967 the Uranium Corporation of India opened India's first uranium mine here. For decades the Jaduguda belt, with nearby mines at Bhatin, Narwapahar and Turamdih, supplied a large part of the fuel for India's nuclear reactors. It has also been the subject of a long dispute. Local groups and some doctors have reported higher rates of birth defects and illness in villages near the tailing ponds; the company and the Department of Atomic Energy have rejected any link to radiation. Independent long-term health studies are still lacking.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The start of India's nuclear fuel chain, and its most contested neighbourhood.
spotlights.memory_hook: India's atomic story begins in a Santhal valley.

spotlights.name: Bokaro Steel Plant
spotlights.spot_it: A vast plant of grey sheds and stacks, built with Russian help, at the centre of a planned township.
spotlights.story_md: Bokaro was India's fourth public sector steel plant, built with the Soviet Union after the United States declined to fund it. Construction began in the late 1960s and the first blast furnace was lit in 1972. Thousands of families from more than 60 villages were moved off the land, and arguments over their jobs and compensation lasted for decades. Bokaro Steel City grew around it as a planned township of sectors. Today the plant is part of SAIL and one of India's biggest producers of flat steel.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Cold War made in steel, in the middle of Jharkhand.
spotlights.memory_hook: America said no, Moscow said yes, Bokaro was born.

sections.title: Three language families in one state
sections.intro_md:
Few places in the world pack three unrelated language families into one small region. Jharkhand does. Santali, Mundari, Ho and Kharia are Austroasiatic, the family of Khmer and Vietnamese. Kurukh, spoken by the Oraons, and Malto, spoken by the Paharias of the Rajmahal hills, are Dravidian. Hindi, Nagpuri (also called Sadri), Khortha, Kurmali, Bengali, Odia and Maithili are Indo-Aryan.

Nagpuri is the bridge. It is the language of the Ranchi bazaar, used between Mundas, Oraons and non-tribals for centuries, and the language of Jharkhand's popular song and film. Khortha does the same job in the north around Dhanbad and Bokaro.

Scripts are a live issue. Most of these languages were first written by missionaries in Roman letters, then in Devanagari or Bengali. In the 20th century tribal intellectuals invented their own: Ol Chiki for Santali in 1925, Warang Citi for Ho in the 1950s. Santali entered the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution in 2003.

data.languages: Hindi, Nagpuri (Sadri), Khortha, Kurmali, Bengali, Odia, Maithili, Magahi, Bhojpuri, Angika, Urdu

spotlights.name: Ol Chiki script
spotlights.spot_it: Rounded letters that look like little pictures, with a sign like a hooked circle; on signs in Santhal towns next to Hindi and English.
spotlights.story_md: Pandit Raghunath Murmu, a Santhal teacher from Mayurbhanj in Odisha, designed Ol Chiki in 1925 because Roman, Bengali and Devanagari letters could not show Santali sounds well. Its 30 letters were designed so that each shape echoes an everyday object or gesture, a way to help learners remember them. In 2003 Santali entered the Eighth Schedule. On 25 December 2025 the Constitution of India was released in Santali in Ol Chiki, and on 29 December 2025 President Droupadi Murmu attended the script's centenary celebration in Jamshedpur. Unicode has supported it since 2008.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A script invented by one man that now carries the Constitution.
spotlights.memory_hook: 100 years old in 2025, and the Constitution in its letters.

sections.title: Groves, jyotirlinga and Jain mountain
sections.intro_md:
In 2011, 12.8 percent of Jharkhandis wrote down a religion that is not on the census form. Most of them meant Sarna: worship centred on the sacred grove (sarna) of sal trees that every Munda and Oraon village keeps, on the village priest called the pahan, on the spirits of ancestors and on a supreme being, Dharmesh or Singbonga. The state assembly asked in 2020 for a separate Sarna code in the census, and in May 2026 Chief Minister Hemant Soren wrote to the Centre again ahead of the 2027 Census.

Jharkhand is also on the main map of Hindu and Jain pilgrimage. Deoghar's Baidyanath temple is one of the twelve jyotirlingas and draws millions each monsoon. Parasnath hill is the holiest place in the Jain world. Rajrappa's headless goddess draws tantric worshippers. Christianity arrived with German Lutherans in 1845 and Belgian Jesuits after 1869, and Ranchi's churches and schools shaped the tribal middle class.

spotlights.name: The sarna grove
spotlights.spot_it: A clump of old sal trees left standing at the village edge, with a white-and-red flag and offerings at the base.
spotlights.story_md: A sarna is a patch of the original forest kept when the village was founded, where the spirits of the place stay. No one cuts its trees. The pahan, the village priest, makes offerings there at Sarhul and other feasts, often sacrificing a chicken and pouring handia. The Sarna flag, a red and white triangle on a pole, now marks groves and homes across Jharkhand. Ecologists point out that these groves have preserved patches of old forest and rare plants for centuries simply because they were sacred.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A religion built around keeping a forest standing.
spotlights.memory_hook: The holiest place in the village is a grove nobody may cut.

spotlights.name: Baidyanath Dham
spotlights.when: Temple in its present form from the 16th century (tradition)
spotlights.spot_it: A tall white temple tower in a crowded courtyard, with pilgrims in saffron carrying water pots on bamboo poles.
spotlights.story_md: Baidyanath is one of the twelve jyotirlingas, the most sacred Shiva shrines, though Parli in Maharashtra makes the same claim. The legend says Ravana was carrying Shiva's linga to Lanka and was tricked into setting it down here. Each Shravan month (July to August), kanwariyas fill pots with Ganga water at Sultanganj in Bihar and walk about 105 kilometres, many barefoot, to pour it on the linga. In 2025 more than 5.2 million pilgrims had offered water by 7 August, with a week of the fair still to run.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of India's biggest annual pilgrimages on foot.
spotlights.memory_hook: A 105-km barefoot walk with a pot of the Ganga.

spotlights.name: Shikharji, Parasnath hill
spotlights.spot_it: A forested hill, the highest in Jharkhand, crowned with small white shrines; pilgrims walking up in the dark before dawn.
spotlights.story_md: Jains believe 20 of the 24 tirthankaras attained moksha on this hill, which makes it the holiest Jain site anywhere. Pilgrims climb about 9 kilometres to the summit at 1,365 metres and walk a circuit of shrines, about 27 kilometres in all, often fasting. The Santhals call the same hill Marang Buru, their great mountain spirit, and hold their own gatherings there. In 2023 a state plan to promote the hill for eco-tourism drew nationwide Jain protests, and the Centre stopped tourism activities on it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Two faiths, one mountain, and a quarrel about tourists.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty saints left the world from this one hill.

spotlights.name: Rajrappa and the headless goddess
spotlights.spot_it: A temple at the meeting of two rivers, with an image of a goddess holding her own severed head.
spotlights.story_md: At Rajrappa the Bhairavi river falls into the Damodar, and on the rocky bank stands a temple to Chhinnamasta, the goddess who cut off her own head to feed her hungry attendants with her blood. The image shows her standing on a couple making love, head in hand, three streams of blood arching out. It is one of the main centres of tantric worship in eastern India, and goat sacrifices are still offered. Couples come to marry here, and in Navratri the crowds are huge.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the most startling images in Hindu art, still worshipped daily.
spotlights.memory_hook: The goddess who feeds others with her own blood.

sections.title: Masks, drums and the dance ground
sections.intro_md:
Every tribal village in Jharkhand has an akhra, an open dance ground under trees, and on festival nights the whole village dances there in long lines, arms linked, swaying to drums. Dance is not a performance for an audience. It is how the village celebrates, courts, mourns and worships, which is why the late scholar Ram Dayal Munda's slogan became famous: 'Je nachi se bachi', those who dance will survive.

The instruments are drums above all: the mandar, a long clay drum with two heads, slung from the shoulder; the nagara, a big kettle drum; the dhol; the tamak and tumdak of the Santhals; and the banam, a one-string fiddle. Songs follow the year: Sarhul songs in spring, Karam songs in the monsoon, Sohrai songs at harvest.

Then there is Chhau, a masked dance-drama. Its refined form grew at the royal court of Seraikela; a showier style with giant headdresses and leaps is danced in Purulia across the Bengal border and in Jharkhand's eastern districts. UNESCO listed Chhau in 2010.

spotlights.name: Chhau, the masked dance
spotlights.when: Royal patronage from the 19th century; UNESCO 2010
spotlights.spot_it: Male dancers in painted masks, to drums and the shehnai: calm, small masks and slow poses at Seraikela; towering, glittering headdresses and leaps in the Purulia style of the eastern border.
spotlights.story_md: Chhau comes from martial drills, and in Seraikela the rajas turned it into a refined masked drama in the 19th and 20th centuries, performed at the Chaitra Parva spring festival. The masks, of papier mache and clay, are calm and stylised, so the whole body must carry the emotion: a swan's neck, a hunter's crouch, Radha's longing. Seraikela, Purulia and Mayurbhanj Chhau were inscribed together on UNESCO's list in 2010. Gurus such as Kedar Nath Sahoo took the form to Europe and America, and the state runs a Chhau dance centre in Seraikela.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Jharkhand's internationally recognised classical-style dance.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dance where the face never moves and the body says everything.

compare.difference: Purulia masks are huge and bright and the dancers leap; Seraikela masks are calm and the movement is slow and lyrical.

spotlights.name: Akhra line dances
spotlights.spot_it: Women in a long curving line, arms linked behind each other's backs, stepping in unison while men drum in the centre.
spotlights.story_md: The commonest dance in Jharkhand has no stage. In the akhra, women link arms in a chain and move forward and back in small precise steps, bending at the knee, while men with mandar and nagara lead from the front or the middle. Each festival has its own rhythms: Jhumar and Domkach among Nagpuri speakers, Lagre and Dahar among Santhals, Karam dances among Oraons. The songs are sung in turns, a verse from the women, a reply from the men. In cities, college students now perform the same chains at fests and weddings.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Dance as everyday village life, not as performance.
spotlights.memory_hook: Arms linked, knees bent, the whole village as one line.

spotlights.name: Mandar, dhamsa and the drums of the plateau
spotlights.spot_it: A long barrel-shaped clay drum slung across the body, a huge kettle drum beaten with sticks, and a carved one-string fiddle.
spotlights.story_md: The mandar is the heartbeat of Nagpuri and Oraon music. Its body is fired clay, so it is light and loud and breaks easily, and the two heads give a deep note on one side and a sharp crack on the other. Players often dance while they play. Drum makers come from specialist families, and good drums are tuned by applying a black paste to the centre of the skin. Santhal music adds the dhamsa, a big kettle drum, the tamak, and the banam fiddle, carved from one piece of wood. Ram Dayal Munda and other artists brought these instruments onto concert stages in the 1980s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The sound that starts every Jharkhandi festival.
spotlights.memory_hook: Clay drum, two voices, played on the move.

sections.title: Painted walls, scrolls, bronze and wild silk
sections.intro_md:
Jharkhand's best-known art is made on walls. Before the harvest festival of Sohrai and before weddings, women in the villages around Hazaribagh paint the outer walls of their mud houses with huge animals, plants and geometric patterns. The tradition got a Geographical Indication in 2020, and it now appears on railway stations, government buildings and Ranchi's walls.

The other crafts are just as particular. In Amadubi, the Paitkar painters make long paper scrolls that tell stories, songs in pictures. Across the state, Malhar metalworkers cast dokra figures with the lost-wax method, a technique as old as the Indus cities. And in the forests, families rear silkworms on asan and arjun trees to make tasar, a wild golden silk. Jharkhand produced about 81 percent of India's tasar in 2015-16, and its raw tasar output rose from about 90 tonnes in 2001 to 1,363 tonnes in 2024-25.

spotlights.name: Sohrai and Khovar wall painting
spotlights.when: GI tag 2020; rooted in prehistoric rock art
spotlights.spot_it: Whole house walls covered in big earth-coloured animals and plants, or scratched black-and-white patterns.
spotlights.story_md: Sohrai paintings are made by women around October and November for the cattle festival: horses, bulls, peacocks and trees in red, yellow, black and white earth, applied with fingers, rags and twig brushes. Khovar is the marriage art, painted in the wedding season: a dark layer of earth over a white one, with patterns scratched through it using a comb or fingers, so the design shows in two colours. Bulu Imam and his family organised the painters into a cooperative and exhibited their work abroad from the 1990s. Both forms received the Geographical Indication tag in 2020.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The living descendant of the Isko rock art.
spotlights.memory_hook: Houses that dress up for harvest and for weddings.

spotlights.name: Paitkar scroll painting
spotlights.spot_it: A long, narrow paper scroll of panels in natural colours, unrolled while the painter sings the story.
spotlights.story_md: In the village of Amadubi, near Ghatshila, a few families of painters called chitrakars make scrolls of handmade paper painted with stone and plant colours. Each scroll tells a story, from the Ramayana to Santhal creation myths, and the painter sings it as he unrolls it, panel by panel. One old practice was linked to death: a painter would visit a bereaved Santhal family with a portrait of the dead person without eyes, and paint in the eyes for a fee, releasing the soul. Today fewer than a few dozen artists still paint, and the state promotes Amadubi as a rural tourism village.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of India's oldest surviving storytelling-painting traditions.
spotlights.memory_hook: A portrait without eyes until the family pays the painter.

spotlights.name: Dokra metal casting
spotlights.spot_it: Rough-textured brass figures of horses, elephants, women carrying pots, with fine wire-like lines on the surface.
spotlights.story_md: Dokra is lost-wax casting. The artisan builds a clay core, wraps it in thin threads of wax to make the pattern, covers it with clay, then heats it so the wax melts out and pours molten brass into the gap. Each mould is broken to release the piece, so no two are the same. The 'dancing girl' of Mohenjo-daro was made the same way about 4,500 years ago. In Jharkhand the Malhar and Thathera communities make it, along with neighbours in Bengal, Odisha and Chhattisgarh.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A Bronze Age technology still in daily use.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every piece is born by breaking its own mould.

spotlights.name: Tasar silk
spotlights.when: Forest sericulture, ancient; Jharkhand leads India
spotlights.spot_it: A coarse, golden-brown silk with a natural sheen, and big hard cocoons hanging in forest trees.
spotlights.story_md: Tasar comes from wild silk moths, Antheraea mylitta, whose caterpillars feed on asan, arjun and sal leaves in the open forest. Tribal families guard the worms on the trees against birds and wasps for weeks, then collect the cocoons, which are boiled and reeled. The silk is thicker and duller than mulberry silk, with a deep gold colour that needs no dye. Official data for 2015-16 put Jharkhand at about 81 percent of India's tasar output, and the state runs a brand, Jharcraft, to sell the fabric.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's wild silk, mostly grown in Jharkhand's forests.
spotlights.memory_hook: Silkworms that live free in the forest, guarded by families.

sections.title: Rice, forest and fire
sections.intro_md:
Jharkhandi food starts with rice and the forest. The plateau grows rice, millets like marua (finger millet), pulses like kurthi (horse gram), and around them the forest supplies a huge pantry: mushrooms, bamboo shoots, more than a hundred kinds of leafy greens called saag, mahua flowers, sal seeds, wild fruit, red ants, honey and fish from the ponds.

Cooking is simple and smoky. Mustard oil is the fat. Dishes are steamed in sal leaves, roasted on coals or fried in iron pans. Everyday meals are rice, dal, a saag and a vegetable. Festival food means fried rice-flour snacks: dhuska, pitha, arsa and chilka roti.

Rice beer, handia, is part of almost every tribal ritual, offered first to the ancestors. Mahua liquor is the other village drink. The towns add the Bihari repertoire, like litti chokha and thekua, and in Jamshedpur and Dhanbad, Bengali sweets.

data.name: Mahua flowers fall, collected at dawn
Rugra from the sal forest floor

spotlights.name: Dhuska
spotlights.spot_it: Deep-fried, puffy, golden discs, crisp outside and soft inside, served with a chickpea or potato curry.
spotlights.story_md: Dhuska is the breakfast of Ranchi's street stalls. Rice and chana dal (sometimes urad) are soaked overnight, ground to a thick batter with green chilli and spices, then ladled into hot mustard oil, where they puff up. It is eaten with ghugni, a curry of black chickpeas or dried peas, or with aloo curry and a sharp chutney. A plate of four with curry costs very little and fills you till lunch. It is also a festival food in Nagpuri and Oraon homes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The one dish every Ranchi visitor should eat.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rice batter, hot oil, puffed gold.

spotlights.name: Rugra
spotlights.spot_it: Small, round, white or grey mushrooms like pebbles, sold in heaps by roadside sellers in the monsoon.
spotlights.story_md: Rugra is a puffball mushroom, mostly species of Astraeus, that grows just under the soil in sal forests after the first heavy rains. Villagers, often women and children, comb the forest floor at dawn to find them by the cracks in the soil. They are cooked as a curry with onions and spices and taste a little like meat, which is why Ranchi calls rugra 'vegetarian mutton'. Prices in the city can rise above those of chicken in a short season. They cannot yet be farmed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A forest food that the city pays a premium for.
spotlights.memory_hook: Vegetarian mutton, dug from under the sal trees.

spotlights.name: Handia
spotlights.spot_it: A milky white, slightly sour rice beer served in leaf cups or bowls from a clay pot.
spotlights.story_md: Handia is made by cooking rice, mixing it with ranu, a starter tablet of rice flour and up to 20 forest roots and herbs, and leaving it in an earthen pot for a few days. The result is a mild, sweet-sour beer. It is offered to ancestors and deities before anyone drinks, served at births, weddings and every festival, and sold by women at weekly markets. Reformers from Birsa Munda to the Tana Bhagats preached against it. Nutritionists note that, in moderation, it carries B vitamins and live microbes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The ritual drink of Jharkhand's Adivasis.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rice, roots and a clay pot: the ancestors drink first.

spotlights.name: Mahua
spotlights.when: Flowers fall in March and April
spotlights.spot_it: Creamy, fleshy flowers carpeting the ground under big trees in spring, swept up into baskets at dawn.
spotlights.story_md: The mahua tree drops its sweet, fleshy flowers at night in March and April, and villagers clear the ground under each tree with fire to collect them each morning. Dried, they are eaten, fed to cattle, and above all distilled into mahua liquor. The seeds give an oil used for cooking and soap. A single big tree can yield over 100 kilograms of flowers in a season, an important cash crop for forest families. The fires lit to clear the ground are also a major cause of Jharkhand's spring forest fires.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A tree that is food, drink, oil and income.
spotlights.memory_hook: The tree that rains sugar at night.

sections.title: A year of festivals
sections.intro_md:
The tribal calendar follows the forest and the paddy field. Spring brings Sarhul, when the sal trees flower. The monsoon brings Karam, when the rice is planted. After the harvest comes Sohrai, for the cattle, and in January Tusu and Mage Parab close the farming year. Each one is celebrated in the akhra with drums, handia and dancing that runs through the night.

Since statehood these festivals have become public events. Sarhul in Ranchi now means a procession of hundreds of thousands, with Sarna flags, through the city centre. Karam is a state holiday. Hul Diwas on 30 June and Birsa Munda's birthday on 15 November are political festivals as much as memorials.

The Hindu calendar runs in parallel: Chhath on the rivers and ponds of Dhanbad and Hazaribagh, Durga Puja pandals in Ranchi and Jamshedpur, and the month-long Shravani Mela in Deoghar, one of the biggest religious gatherings in India every year.

data.name: Tusu and Makar Sankranti; Mage Parab of the Hos
Chaitra Parva and Chhau at Seraikela
Hul Diwas, 30 June; Rath Yatra in Ranchi
Sohrai after Diwali; Statehood day, 15 November

spotlights.name: Sarhul
spotlights.spot_it: Men and women with white sal flowers tucked behind their ears, red-and-white Sarna flags, a huge procession through Ranchi.
spotlights.story_md: Sarhul celebrates the marriage of the sun and the earth, and the new year, when the sal trees blossom. The pahan fasts, then at the sarna grove places two pots of water. Next morning he reads the water level: if it has stayed high, the rains will be good. Sal flowers are offered and given to every household, and people wear them in their hair. Then the dancing begins. In Ranchi a procession from dozens of akhras fills the city's main roads with drums and flags, an event that has grown hugely since statehood.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The festival that tells the village whether the rains will come.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two pots of water forecast the monsoon.

spotlights.name: Karam
spotlights.spot_it: A leafy branch of the karam tree planted in the middle of the dance ground, with women and girls dancing around it all night.
spotlights.story_md: Young men cut branches of the karam tree, Haldina cordifolia, and bring them dancing into the village. The branch is planted in the akhra, and a storyteller tells the tale of the brothers Karma and Dharma: one neglected the karam deity and lost everything until he made amends. Sisters fast and pray for their brothers' wellbeing, and sprout grain in baskets for days beforehand as a sign of fertility. The dancing lasts till dawn, when the branch is carried to a river or pond and floated away.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The great monsoon festival of the Oraons, Mundas and Sadan communities.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tree branch is the guest of honour for one night.

spotlights.name: Sohrai
spotlights.when: October or November, after the harvest
spotlights.spot_it: Cattle with painted horns and garlands, houses freshly plastered and painted with bold animals.
spotlights.story_md: Sohrai is the festival of thanks to the cattle that plough the fields. Houses are cleaned and replastered, and the women paint the walls. On the main day cattle are bathed, their horns oiled and painted, and they are fed special food. Among the Santhals, Sohrai is the biggest festival of the year and lasts five days, with visits to married daughters and nights of dancing. Some villages hold a game in which a bull is tied to a post and provoked to charge, a test of nerve for young men.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The harvest festival that gives Jharkhand's famous wall art its name.
spotlights.memory_hook: A festival where the bullocks are the guests.

spotlights.name: Tusu Parab
spotlights.spot_it: Tall towers of coloured paper and bamboo, the chaudal, carried to a river by groups of singing women.
spotlights.story_md: Tusu is the harvest festival of the Kurmi Mahto and other communities of the eastern plateau, shared with Purulia in Bengal. For a month before Makar Sankranti, unmarried girls sing Tusu songs every evening to an image of Tusu, imagined as a young girl. On the last day they carry elaborately decorated paper towers called chaudal to the river and immerse them. Tusu songs are famous for being witty and topical: they comment on village scandals, politics and the price of things.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A festival built on women's improvised songs.
spotlights.memory_hook: Songs of gossip and a paper tower floated downriver.

spotlights.name: Shravani Mela
spotlights.spot_it: Long lines of pilgrims in saffron carrying decorated pots slung from a bamboo pole on their shoulders.
spotlights.story_md: During the Hindu month of Shravan, pilgrims called kanwariyas take water from the Ganga at Sultanganj in Bihar and carry it about 105 kilometres to Baidyanath Dham. The pots must not touch the ground on the way. A tougher group, the dak bam, try to cover the whole distance in 24 hours without stopping. Rest camps, medical posts and police line the route. The state counted more than 5.2 million pilgrims by 7 August 2025, with days still to go. Traffic accidents involving pilgrims are a recurring tragedy on the roads around Deoghar.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the largest annual walking pilgrimages in the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: 105 km, and the pot must never touch the ground.

sections.title: How people live
sections.intro_md:
A tribal village in Jharkhand is run by its own institutions. Among the Mundas, the village head is the munda and the priest is the pahan; groups of villages form a parha led by a manki or raja. Among the Santhals the manjhi leads, with a council of elders. These councils still settle land disputes, marriages and fines, and since PESA rules were notified in 2025 and 2026 the gram sabha has formal power over local resources in Fifth Schedule areas, which cover 13 districts fully and two partly.

Women's position is visible and complicated. Tribal women work the fields, run the weekly haat stalls and dance publicly; bride price, not dowry, was the norm. But inheritance customs mostly give land to sons, and witch-hunting, in which women are branded dayan and attacked, still kills people every year despite a 2001 state law against it.

Migration is the other fact of life. Every year hundreds of thousands of Jharkhandis go to work in brick kilns, construction and homes from Delhi to Kerala.

spotlights.name: Pathalgadi, the stone slabs
spotlights.spot_it: Large painted green stone slabs at village entrances, carved with lines from the Constitution.
spotlights.story_md: Mundas and Hos have always raised stones: over graves, to mark boundaries, to record a lineage. In 2017 and 2018 villages around Khunti began erecting big green slabs inscribed with Fifth Schedule provisions and PESA, declaring the gram sabha sovereign and barring outsiders. The state government of the day called it anti-national, and police filed sedition cases that, by press counts, named thousands of villagers. After Hemant Soren's government took office in December 2019, its first cabinet decision was to withdraw the Pathalgadi cases.
spotlights.why_it_matters: An ancient custom turned into a constitutional protest.
spotlights.memory_hook: The village wrote the Constitution on a rock.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
Jharkhand's best-known modern names are sportspeople, and that is not an accident. The Jesuit and Lutheran schools of Ranchi, Gumla and Simdega took up hockey in the early 20th century, and the region has been sending players to India's teams ever since, from Jaipal Singh Munda in 1928 to Sylvanus Dung Dung in 1980 and a long line of women players from Simdega today. The steel companies built stadiums and academies: Tata Steel's archery and football academies in Jamshedpur, and the Keenan Stadium.

Beyond sport, Jharkhand's people to know include soldiers, scholars and singers. The list below is short. Also worth knowing: Draupadi Murmu served as Jharkhand's first woman Governor from 2015 to 2021 before becoming President.

spotlights.name: MS Dhoni
spotlights.spot_it: A wicketkeeper with a calm face, a helicopter shot, and once long hair; Ranchi's most famous son.
spotlights.story_md: Mahendra Singh Dhoni grew up in a Mecon staff colony in Ranchi, kept goal for his school football team and was turned into a wicketkeeper by a coach. He worked as a ticket collector at Kharagpur railway station while playing first-class cricket for Bihar and then Jharkhand. He led India to the World T20 in 2007, the 50-over World Cup in 2011 and the Champions Trophy in 2013, the only captain to win all three ICC white-ball trophies. He still lives in Ranchi, where his farmhouse and bike collection are local legends.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that a small-town Jharkhandi could lead Indian cricket.
spotlights.memory_hook: A ticket collector who collected three world trophies.

spotlights.name: Deepika Kumari
spotlights.spot_it: A recurve archer at full draw, string touching her chin, often in India's national colours.
spotlights.story_md: Deepika Kumari is the daughter of an autorickshaw driver and a nurse from a village near Ranchi. As a child she practised by shooting stones at mangoes. She joined the Tata Archery Academy in Jamshedpur in 2006 and won the Youth World Championship in 2009. In 2012 she became the world number one in women's recurve. She has won Commonwealth gold, many World Cup golds and the Padma Shri in 2016, and has competed at four Olympics. Her story is told in the documentary Ladies First (2017).
spotlights.why_it_matters: The best-known Indian archer of her generation, from a Jharkhand village.
spotlights.memory_hook: From mangoes to world number one.

spotlights.name: Albert Ekka, Param Vir Chakra
spotlights.spot_it: A young Lance Naik in Brigade of the Guards uniform on a postage stamp and statues across Jharkhand.
spotlights.story_md: Albert Ekka, an Oraon from the village of Jari in Gumla, joined the Bihar Regiment and later the Brigade of the Guards. On the night of 3 December 1971, at the start of the war with Pakistan, his battalion attacked Pakistani positions at Gangasagar near Agartala. Though wounded, he charged a bunker and silenced a machine gun, then climbed to a second gun position and silenced that too before he died of his wounds. He received the Param Vir Chakra after death, the only Jharkhandi so far to win India's highest gallantry award.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Jharkhand's only Param Vir Chakra.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two machine guns silenced in one night at Gangasagar.

spotlights.name: Ram Dayal Munda
spotlights.spot_it: A smiling man with a mandar drum or flute, leading a troupe of dancers on a concert stage.
spotlights.story_md: Ram Dayal Munda studied linguistics and anthropology at the University of Chicago and taught in Minnesota before coming home in 1981 to build the Department of Tribal and Regional Languages at Ranchi University, later serving as its Vice-Chancellor. He was a musician, flautist and dancer who took Jharkhand's akhra culture to world stages, a theorist of the statehood movement and a voice for Adivasi rights at the UN. He coined the line 'Je nachi se bachi', those who dance will survive. He received the Padma Shri in 2010.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The scholar who made tribal culture a university subject.
spotlights.memory_hook: From Chicago to Ranchi, with a flute and a slogan.

spotlights.name: Jamsetji Tata
spotlights.spot_it: A heavy-set man with a white beard and a Parsi cap; a statue in the middle of Jamshedpur.
spotlights.story_md: Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata was a Bombay textile industrialist who set out four goals: a steel plant, a hydroelectric plant, a world-class science institute and a great hotel. He lived to open only the Taj Mahal hotel in 1903. Before he died in 1904 he wrote to his son about the steel town he imagined, with wide streets, shade trees, space for football and hockey, and areas for temples, mosques and churches. Jamshedpur was laid out along those lines, and his birthday, 3 March, is celebrated as Founder's Day with lights in Jubilee Park.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The man whose idea built Jharkhand's biggest city.
spotlights.memory_hook: He wrote a letter about a city, and then a city appeared.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Jharkhand is one of India's least visited states, and that is part of the appeal. A first trip usually starts in Ranchi, with a day for the waterfalls, Hundru, Dassam and Jonha, and an evening on Tagore Hill. From there: Netarhat and Betla for forest and sunset, two to three days. Deoghar for Baidyanath, Parasnath for the Jain hill, Maluti for the temples, a week if you combine them. Jamshedpur for the planned city, Jubilee Park and the Dalma hills.

The best season is October to March. The monsoon, July to September, is when the falls are at their best and the forest is green, but roads can wash out. April to June is hot, above 40 degrees in Palamu, though Ranchi stays milder.

Worth a detour: McCluskieganj, a forest town built for Anglo-Indians, and Tagore Hill in Ranchi, home of Rabindranath Tagore's brother Jyotirindranath from 1908 to 1925.

spotlights.name: McCluskieganj

where.label: Ranchi district, about 65 km north-west of Ranchi

spotlights.spot_it: Big old bungalows with verandas and tiled roofs scattered in sal forest, some empty, some turned into guest houses.
spotlights.story_md: In 1933 Ernest Timothy McCluskie, an Anglo-Indian businessman from Calcutta, set up the Colonisation Society of India and bought land from the Raja of Ratu to create a homeland, a 'mooluk', for Anglo-Indians, who felt they belonged neither to Britain nor to India. Within ten years about 400 families had come. After the Second World War and independence most left for Australia, Britain and Canada. A handful of families stayed. Today McCluskieganj is a quiet town of about 3,000 people, with its bungalows as weekend homes and a Don Bosco school.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A planned homeland for a community that had nowhere else.
spotlights.memory_hook: A forest town built for a people who then emigrated.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
Hemant Soren of the JMM won a second consecutive term in November 2024, the first time a Jharkhand government was re-elected. His alliance's big promise was the Maiyan Samman scheme, a monthly cash transfer to women aged 18 to 50, now 2,500 rupees and the largest single item in the 1.58 lakh crore rupee budget for 2026-27.

2025 was a year of anniversaries and loss. Shibu Soren died on 4 August. On 15 November the state marked its silver jubilee and the 150th birth anniversary of Birsa Munda. In December the Constitution appeared in Santali in Ol Chiki and the script turned 100.

The long Maoist war is ending. Security forces pushed deep into Saranda and the Kolhan in 2025 and 2026; in March 2026 Union Home Minister Amit Shah told the Lok Sabha that all main armed Maoist cadres had been finished, and on 28 July 2026 Misir Besra, the last major absconding leader, was arrested on the Dhanbad-Giridih border. Big questions remain on land, mining and identity: Saranda's sanctuary, the PESA rules and the Sarna code for the 2027 Census.

spotlights.name: Hemant Soren
spotlights.when: Chief Minister since 2019 (with a break in 2024)
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded man in a kurta and waistcoat, often with a green JMM stole, addressing crowds in Santali and Hindi.
spotlights.story_md: Hemant Soren, Shibu Soren's son, first became Chief Minister in 2013, then again in December 2019. In January 2024 he was arrested by the Enforcement Directorate in a land case and resigned; he spent five months in jail, was granted bail by the Jharkhand High Court, which said there was no prima facie evidence against him, and returned as Chief Minister in July 2024. In November 2024 his alliance won 56 of the 81 assembly seats, the first re-election of a sitting government in the state's history. His wife Kalpana Soren is also an MLA.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
Jharkhand suffers from three lazy images: a jungle full of Maoists, a coal pit, and a part of Bihar. Each holds a grain of truth and each misleads. The Maoist insurgency was real and deadly, but most of the state never saw fighting and the armed movement is now nearly finished. Coal matters, but so do steel, silk, education and a big services economy in Ranchi and Jamshedpur. And Jharkhand was a distinct cultural region long before 2000: its languages, laws and festivals were never Bihar's.

The table sets out what the evidence says on a few smaller myths too.

data.fact: Scheduled Tribes were 26.2% in 2011. About three-quarters of people are non-tribal.
Christians were 4.3% of the state in 2011. Most tribal people follow Sarna or Hindu practice.

data.myth: Jharkhand's languages are dialects of Hindi
data.fact: Santali, Mundari and Ho are Austroasiatic and Kurukh is Dravidian. They are not related to Hindi.

data.myth: Sloth bears get drunk on fallen mahua flowers
data.fact: A popular story. Bears do eat mahua flowers, but there is no scientific evidence of drunken bears.

data.myth: The Jharia fire is a natural disaster
data.fact: Most fires spread through badly abandoned private workings and illegal mining. It is man-made.

data.myth: Netarhat's Magnolia Point is named after a real woman
data.fact: The love story is local folklore with no documentary record.

data.myth: Tribal land can be bought like any other land
data.fact: The CNT and SPT Acts bar most sales of tribal land to non-tribals.

sections.title: Recap
sections.intro_md:
Jharkhand, the land of forests, was carved from Bihar on 15 November 2000, Birsa Munda's birthday. It sits on the Chota Nagpur Plateau, where rivers fall off rock steps into waterfalls: Hundru, Dassam, Jonha and Lodh, the highest at about 143 metres. Under it lies a quarter of India's coal and iron, its only prime coking coal at Jharia, burning since 1916, and its first uranium at Jaduguda. On top, Jamshedpur, India's first planned steel city.

A quarter of the people are Adivasi: Santhals, Mundas, Oraons and Hos, speaking Austroasiatic and Dravidian languages, worshipping at sarna groves, dancing in the akhra. They rose again and again: Tilka Manjhi, the Kol uprising, the Santhal Hul of 1855, Birsa's Ulgulan, the Tana Bhagats. Their reward was land law, the CNT Act of 1908, and a century later, a state.

Remember the painted Sohrai walls, Seraikela's masks, tasar silk, dhuska and rugra, Baidyanath's 105-kilometre walk and Shikharji's 20 saints.

best_facts.fact: The coal under Jharia has been on fire since at least 1916, and by 2007 about 37 million tonnes had burned while 400,000 people lived on ground at risk of collapse.
best_facts.why_surprising: A town has sat on a fire for over a century.

best_facts.fact: Jharkhand was created on 15 November 2000, chosen because it was the birth anniversary of Birsa Munda, a rebel who died in a British jail at about 25.
best_facts.why_surprising: A state's birthday is a rebel's birthday.

best_facts.fact: Kurukh, the language of Jharkhand's Oraons, is Dravidian: its closest relatives are spoken in south India, not by its Hindi-speaking neighbours.
best_facts.why_surprising: A south Indian language family in the middle of the north.

best_facts.fact: Jainism's holiest site is in Jharkhand: Jains believe 20 of the 24 tirthankaras attained moksha on Parasnath hill.
best_facts.why_surprising: Most people place Jain heartlands in Gujarat and Rajasthan.

best_facts.fact: Jaipal Singh Munda, an Oxford-educated Munda, captained India at the 1928 Olympics, the first time India won hockey gold, and later led the first movement for a Jharkhand state.
best_facts.why_surprising: An Olympic captain founded a statehood movement.

best_facts.fact: In 1932 a forest officer in Palamau counted tigers by their pugmarks, often described as the world's first tiger census. Palamau now has only one or a few tigers.
best_facts.why_surprising: The place that first counted tigers nearly lost them.

best_facts.fact: Jamshedpur has no elected municipal corporation: Tata Steel's subsidiary has run its water, roads and power for more than a century.
best_facts.why_surprising: A city of over a million run by a company.

best_facts.fact: India's first uranium mine opened at Jaduguda in 1967.
best_facts.why_surprising: India's nuclear fuel starts in a tribal valley in Jharkhand.

best_facts.fact: The Ol Chiki script for Santali was invented by one man, Raghunath Murmu, in 1925. In December 2025 the Constitution of India was released in Santali in that script.
best_facts.why_surprising: A one-man alphabet now carries the Constitution.

best_facts.fact: Every Shravan, millions of pilgrims carry Ganga water about 105 km on foot from Sultanganj to Deoghar; over 5.2 million had done so by 7 August 2025.
best_facts.why_surprising: One of the biggest annual walks on earth.

best_facts.fact: Paitkar painters of Amadubi once brought a grieving Santhal family a portrait of the dead person with no eyes, and painted the eyes in for a fee to free the soul.
best_facts.why_surprising: Art as a service for the dead.

best_facts.fact: Women in Hazaribagh still paint their houses with patterns very similar to those in the nearby Isko rock shelter, whose art is thought to be thousands of years old.
best_facts.why_surprising: A possible unbroken art line across millennia.

best_facts.fact: Jharkhand produced about 81 percent of India's tasar silk in 2015-16, spun by wild silkworms raised on forest trees.
best_facts.why_surprising: Most Indian 'Tussar' saris start in Jharkhand's forests.

best_facts.fact: At Punkri Barwadih, near Hazaribagh, crowds gather each equinox to watch the sun rise in the V-shaped gap between two ancient standing stones.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Stonehenge-style alignment that few Indians know.

best_facts.fact: The Mughals cared about Chota Nagpur for its river diamonds, and the Nagvanshi king Durjan Shah is said to have won release from 12 years in a Mughal prison by spotting a real diamond.
best_facts.why_surprising: Freedom bought with an expert eye.

best_facts.fact: Rugra, a puffball mushroom dug from sal forests in the monsoon, is nicknamed 'vegetarian mutton' in Ranchi and can sell for more than chicken.
best_facts.why_surprising: A forest fungus priced above meat.

best_facts.fact: McCluskieganj was founded in 1933 as a homeland for Anglo-Indians; about 400 families came within a decade, and most later emigrated.
best_facts.why_surprising: A forest town in Jharkhand built for one small community.

best_facts.fact: MS Dhoni worked as a ticket collector at Kharagpur station while playing first-class cricket for Jharkhand's region, and became the only captain to win all three ICC white-ball trophies.
best_facts.why_surprising: From railway platform to three world titles.

quiz_bank.explanation: Lodh Falls, about 143 m, in Latehar.

quiz_bank.prompt: Tap the Saranda forest.
quiz_bank.explanation: In West Singhbhum, in the far south-west of the Kolhan.

quiz_bank.prompt: Which group speaks a Dravidian language?
quiz_bank.explanation: The Oraons speak Kurukh, a Dravidian language.

quiz_bank.prompt: How many temples survive at Maluti of the original 108?
quiz_bank.explanation: 72 survive.

quiz_bank.prompt: Which day is Hul Diwas?
quiz_bank.explanation: 30 June, the start of the Santhal Hul in 1855.

quiz_bank.prompt: Birsa Munda died in Ranchi jail in 1900 at about 25.
quiz_bank.explanation: He died on 9 June 1900.

quiz_bank.prompt: Jaipal Singh Munda captained India's hockey team at which Olympics?
quiz_bank.explanation: Amsterdam 1928.

quiz_bank.prompt: In which year was the first Jharia mine fire recorded?
quiz_bank.explanation: 1916, at Bhowrah colliery.

quiz_bank.prompt: Jamsetji Tata lived to see the first steel poured at Jamshedpur.
quiz_bank.explanation: He died in 1904; the first ingot came in 1912.

quiz_bank.prompt: When did Raghunath Murmu create Ol Chiki?
quiz_bank.explanation: 1925; the centenary was celebrated in 2025.

quiz_bank.prompt: How many tirthankaras do Jains believe attained moksha on Parasnath hill?
quiz_bank.explanation: Twenty of the twenty-four.

quiz_bank.prompt: Chhau was inscribed by UNESCO in 2010.
quiz_bank.explanation: Seraikela, Purulia and Mayurbhanj Chhau together.

quiz_bank.prompt: Khovar wall painting is made mainly for which occasion?
quiz_bank.explanation: Weddings. Sohrai is for the harvest cattle festival.

quiz_bank.prompt: Jharkhand's share of India's tasar silk in 2015-16 was higher or lower than 50 percent?
quiz_bank.explanation: About 81 percent.

quiz_bank.prompt: Rugra is nicknamed what in Ranchi?
quiz_bank.explanation: 'Vegetarian mutton'.

quiz_bank.prompt: At Sarhul the pahan forecasts the monsoon from water left in pots.
quiz_bank.explanation: If the water level holds, the rains will be good.

quiz_bank.prompt: What did Pathalgadi villages inscribe on their stones in 2017 and 2018?
quiz_bank.explanation: Constitutional provisions on Scheduled Areas and gram sabhas.

quiz_bank.prompt: MS Dhoni once worked as a ticket collector at Kharagpur station.
quiz_bank.explanation: From about 2001 to 2003, while playing first-class cricket.

quiz_bank.prompt: In March 2026, what did Amit Shah tell the Lok Sabha?
quiz_bank.explanation: That all main armed Maoist cadres had been finished.
options: The armed Maoist movement had been wiped out

quiz_bank.prompt: Most Adivasis in Jharkhand are Christian.
quiz_bank.explanation: Christians were 4.3 percent of the state in 2011; most tribal people follow Sarna or Hindu practice.

side_dish.title: How to invent an alphabet: Ol Chiki
side_dish.body_md:
Most of the world's scripts grew slowly over centuries. Ol Chiki was designed by one person. Raghunath Murmu, a Santhal teacher born in 1905 in Mayurbhanj, Odisha, faced a practical problem: Santali was being written in Roman letters by missionaries, in Bengali in Bengal, in Odia in Odisha and in Devanagari in Bihar. None of them handled Santali's sounds well, such as its checked consonants and its glottal stops, and none of them belonged to Santhals.

In 1925 he finished a new script of 30 letters. Two design choices stand out. First, it is a true alphabet, like Greek or Latin: vowels are full letters, not marks attached to consonants as in Devanagari, which suits the way Santali words are built. Second, each letter's shape was linked to a familiar object or action, which made the script easy to teach in village schools.

Adoption took decades and followed politics. The script spread through Santhal cultural societies, then state recognition in Odisha, Jharkhand and West Bengal, then Unicode in 2008, which put it on phones. In December 2025 the Constitution of India was released in Santali in Ol Chiki, a century after its invention.

The lesson for anyone who designs systems: a script succeeds less on elegance than on identity and institutions. Ol Chiki won because people wanted letters of their own and built schools, presses and fonts to carry them.

offline_task.title: Make dhuska tonight
offline_task.body_md: Soak 1 cup of rice and half a cup of chana dal separately for 6 hours or overnight. Drain and grind together with 2 green chillies, a small piece of ginger and a little water into a thick, slightly coarse batter, thicker than dosa batter. Stir in salt, half a teaspoon of turmeric and a pinch of cumin. Heat mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes, then lower the heat a little. Drop in a ladle of batter at a time; each dhuska should puff and float. Fry until golden on both sides and drain. Serve hot with ghugni (black chickpeas cooked with onion, tomato and garam masala) or a simple potato curry, and a green chutney. As you eat, remember: this is breakfast on Ranchi's Main Road, a city on top of a plateau of waterfalls.
